heroText: Brasilia is Brazil's planned capital, built around sweeping avenues, monumental government buildings and Oscar Niemeyer's modernist architecture. Follow the Eixo Monumental from the Cathedral of Brasilia to the National Congress and Praca dos Tres Poderes, then cross to Pontao do Lago Sul for lake views. Brasilia airport sits close enough for straightforward transfers.

areas.name: Setor Hoteleiro Sul
areas.text: Setor Hoteleiro Sul is the classic hotel base, close to ministries, malls and the Eixo Monumental by taxi or rideshare.

areas.name: Setor Hoteleiro Norte
areas.text: Setor Hoteleiro Norte has many business hotels and quick access to shopping, convention venues and central government districts.

areas.name: Asa Sul
areas.text: Asa Sul feels more local and residential, with restaurants, cafes and easier evenings than the formal hotel sectors.

areas.name: Asa Norte
areas.text: Asa Norte is useful for university visits, casual bars and a less formal stay while remaining close to central roads.

areas.name: Lago Sul
areas.text: Lago Sul is quieter and upscale, best for lake restaurants, embassies and car-based stays outside the monumental core.

airports.name: Brasilia International Airport (BSB)
airports.text: Brasilia International Airport sits south of the Plano Piloto; transfers are usually straightforward, but government traffic can slow central routes.

airportTransfer.value: 20-35 min by taxi or ride-hail to the Plano Piloto hotel sectors
airportTransfer.distance: about 12 km south of the central axis

stayOverview: Use Setor Hoteleiro Sul or Norte for the easiest monument and business access, then compare Asa Sul or Asa Norte for more restaurants and local evenings. Lago Sul suits quieter, car-based stays near lake dining and embassies.
hotelIntro: Brasilia hotel choice depends on purpose: the hotel sectors are practical but formal, Asa Sul and Asa Norte feel more lived-in, and Lago Sul works when lake views, embassies or quieter nights matter more than walking.
rentalCars: A rental car helps in Brasilia because distances are wide and many sights sit along car-oriented avenues.

travelTips.title: Distances
travelTips.text: Do not judge Brasilia by map distance alone; roads are broad, crossings are limited and many routes work better by car.

travelTips.title: Best base
travelTips.text: Choose the hotel sectors for business or short stays, then use Asa Sul for restaurants and a more local evening routine.

travelTips.title: Architecture route
travelTips.text: Plan the Cathedral, National Congress and Praca dos Tres Poderes as one axis rather than scattered stops.

travelTips.title: Dry season
travelTips.text: The dry months can feel very dusty and bright, so carry water, sunglasses and sun protection for monument walks.

highlights.title: Cathedral of Brasilia
highlights.text: The Cathedral of Brasilia is one of Niemeyer's defining works, with sculptural concrete ribs and a striking stained-glass interior.

highlights.title: National Congress
highlights.text: The National Congress anchors the Eixo Monumental with twin towers and bowl-shaped chambers that define the capital's skyline.

highlights.title: Praca dos Tres Poderes
highlights.text: Praca dos Tres Poderes brings the presidential palace, Supreme Court and Congress together in Brasilia's symbolic civic space.

highlights.title: Juscelino Kubitschek Memorial
highlights.text: Juscelino Kubitschek Memorial is a named Brasilia landmark that helps structure a real visit, adding orientation, local context and a clear route anchor.

highlights.title: Santuario Dom Bosco
highlights.text: Santuario Dom Bosco is famous for its blue stained glass, a calm and memorable stop away from the main axis.

highlights.title: Pontao do Lago Sul
highlights.text: Pontao do Lago Sul is the easy lakefront dining and sunset stop, especially useful after a day of monuments.

nearbyIdeas.name: Chapada dos Veadeiros
nearbyIdeas.label: Nature
nearbyIdeas.text: Chapada dos Veadeiros is a major cerrado and waterfall escape, better as a weekend than a quick day trip.

nearbyIdeas.name: Pirenopolis
nearbyIdeas.label: Heritage
nearbyIdeas.text: Pirenopolis is a heritage-focused side trip from Brasilia; check the route and opening hours before setting aside the day.

nearbyIdeas.name: Cristalina
nearbyIdeas.label: Nature
nearbyIdeas.text: Cristalina is known for quartz, rural scenery and outdoor stops southeast of Brasilia, easiest with a car.

history.text: Stating that "The Union shall own, in the central plateau of the Republic, an area of 14,400 square kilometers, which will be demarcated in due course to establish the future federal capital." The government.
The idea of relocating Brazil's capital city was conceived in 1827 by José Bonifácio, an advisor to Emperor Pedro I.
According to a legend, Italian saint Don Bosco in 1883 had a dream in which he described a futuristic city that roughly fitted Brasília's location.
After the Proclamation of the Republic, the Third Article of the new Constitution from 1891 stated that the capital should be moved from Rio de Janeiro to a place close to the country's center.
Already in 1892, the astronomer Louis Cruls, in the service of the Brazilian government, had investigated the site for the future capital.

history.label: 20th century
history.text: Though automobiles were invented prior to the 20th century, mass production of vehicles in the early 20th made them widely available; thus, they became a symbol of modernity.

In 1922 to celebrate the 100th anniversary of Brazil's independence, President Epitácio Pessoa ordered the construction of an obelisk in the Cruls Quadrilateral, known as the Foundation Stone of Brasília, to mark the location.
Upon taking office in January 1956, in fulfilment of his campaign pledge, he initiated the planning and construction of the new capital.

history.label: Modern city
history.text: Brasilia's geographically central location fostered a more regionally neutral federal capital.

history.label: Civic role
history.text: He presented a plan to the General Assembly of Brazil for a new city called Brasília, with the idea of moving the capital westward from the heavily populated southeastern corridor.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: In Brasília today, many references to Bosco, who founded the Salesian order, are found throughout the city and one church parish in the city bears his name.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: But one can not ignore the bus transportation system in the city.

history.label: Regional role
